title: Cost of Living Compare: Same Life, Two Cities
description: Compare cost of living between two cities with Cost of Living Compare — index logic explained so the numbers stay honest. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, on index arithmetic alone, a $3,000 monthly budget in a city indexed at 92 needs about $5,870 in a city indexed at 180 to buy the same life — the indexes are illustrative; the method is the lesson.
quick_answer: Cost of Living Compare sets two cities' living costs side by side using index numbers — each city's basket price relative to a common baseline. Pick the pair and read what the same life costs there versus here — and what a salary buys in each.

examples.label: Example · How to read an index

body.t: Index 100 is the baseline basket. A city at 180 costs 1.8 times the baseline for the same basket; at 92, about 8 percent less. Salary equivalence runs the ratio backward: multiply by (destination ÷ current) — the worked budget in the summary is that arithmetic, with illustrative indexes.

Indexes average the basket; your life may not. A renter's comparison is dominated by the housing row, a homeowner's by everything else. Read the category rows, not just the headline — the tool shows both because the headline alone misleads most movers.

popular_table.note: Cost-of-living indexes (the C2ER/ACCRA tradition in the US) price a basket for a reference household. They are comparison instruments, not predictions of your spending — your basket is your own.

faq: Is the comparison official inflation data?

No — it is a cross-city price index, not a time-series inflation measure (that is the CPI's job, and the base FAQ names the distinction). City-versus-city and month-versus-month are different questions.
The index family's reference — a national average basket in the C2ER tradition. Both cities are measured against the same 100, which is what makes their ratio meaningful.
Why is my experience different from the index?

The basket belongs to a reference household. Childcare, a car habit, or a taste for eating out reweights your personal index — the category rows let you recompute the comparison with your own weights.
Price indexes price goods and housing, not tax codes. Two cities with equal indexes can leave different paycheques after state, city and sales taxes — treat tax as a second, separate comparison.
Index publishers survey periodically; rents in hot markets outrun any survey. Use the comparison for the decision's scale (a 90-point gap is decisive; a 4-point gap is noise).
Indexes are city-level. Neighbourhood rents can double across one city — the index frames the negotiation; the neighbourhood decides it.
Cross-border comparisons add currency and basket-definition differences; treat them as orientation, and convert at a stated exchange-rate date.
Quote the ratio, not a vibe: 'the destination indexes 1.4× my current city on the same basket' is a sentence a manager can take to finance.
